nodes.name: IsPicardLindelof.exists_eq_forall_mem_Icc_hasDerivWithinAt
nodes.lean:
existence of a local solution whose initial point `x` may be different from the centre `x₀` of
the closed ball within which the properties of the vector field hold. -/
theorem exists_eq_forall_mem_Icc_hasDerivWithinAt
    (hf : IsPicardLindelof f t₀ x₀ a r L K) (hx : x ∈ closedBall x₀ r) :
    ∃ α : ℝ → E, α t₀ = x ∧
      ∀ t ∈ Icc tmin tmax, HasDerivWithinAt α (f t (α t)) (Icc tmin tmax) t := by
  obtain ⟨α, hα⟩ := FunSpace.exists_isFixedPt_next hf hx
  refine ⟨α.compProj, by rw [FunSpace.compProj_val, ← hα, FunSpace.next_apply₀], fun t ht ↦ ?_⟩
  apply hasDerivWithinAt_picard_Icc t₀.property hf.continuousOn_uncurry
    α.continuous_compProj.continuousOn (fun _ ht' ↦ α.compProj_mem_closedBall hf.mul_max_le)
    x ht |>.congr_of_mem _ ht
  intro t' ht'

theorem ODE_solution_unique_of_mem_Icc
    (hv : ∀ t ∈ Ioo a b, LipschitzOnWith K (v t) (s t))
    (ht : t₀ ∈ Ioo a b)
    (hf : ContinuousOn f (Icc a b))
    (hf' : ∀ t ∈ Ioo a b, HasDerivAt f (v t (f t)) t)
    (hfs : ∀ t ∈ Ioo a b, f t ∈ s t)
    (hg : ContinuousOn g (Icc a b))
    (hg' : ∀ t ∈ Ioo a b, HasDerivAt g (v t (g t)) t)
    (hgs : ∀ t ∈ Ioo a b, g t ∈ s t)
    (heq : f t₀ = g t₀) :
    EqOn f g (Icc a b) := by
  rw [← Icc_union_Icc_eq_Icc (le_of_lt ht.1) (le_of_lt ht.2)]
  apply EqOn.union
  · have hss : Ioc a t₀ ⊆ Ioo a b := Ioc_subset_Ioo_right ht.2
    exact ODE_solution_unique_of_mem_Icc_left (fun t ht ↦ hv t (hss ht))
      (hf.mono <| Icc_subset_Icc_right <| le_of_lt ht.2)
      (fun _ ht' ↦ (hf' _ (hss ht')).hasDerivWithinAt) (fun _ ht' ↦ (hfs _ (hss ht')))
      (hg.mono <| Icc_subset_Icc_right <| le_of_lt ht.2)
      (fun _ ht' ↦ (hg' _ (hss ht')).hasDerivWithinAt) (fun _ ht' ↦ (hgs _ (hss ht'))) heq
  · have hss : Ico t₀ b ⊆ Ioo a b := Ico_subset_Ioo_left ht.1
    exact ODE_solution_unique_of_mem_Icc_right (fun t ht ↦ hv t (hss ht))
      (hf.mono <| Icc_subset_Icc_left <| le_of_lt ht.1)
      (fun _ ht' ↦ (hf' _ (hss ht')).hasDerivWithinAt) (fun _ ht' ↦ (hfs _ (hss ht')))
      (hg.mono <| Icc_subset_Icc_left <| le_of_lt ht.1)
      (fun _ ht' ↦ (hg' _ (hss ht')).hasDerivWithinAt) (fun _ ht' ↦ (hgs _ (hss ht'))) heq

nodes.name: IsPicardLindelof
nodes.lean:
`IsPicardLindelof f t₀ x₀ a r L K`, where `t₀ ∈ Icc tmin tmax`, means that the time-dependent vector
field `f` satisfies the conditions to admit an integral curve `α : ℝ → E` to `f` defined on
`Icc tmin tmax` with the initial condition `α t₀ = x`, where `‖x - x₀‖ ≤ r`. Note that the initial
point `x` is allowed to differ from the point `x₀` about which the conditions on `f` are stated. -/
structure IsPicardLindelof {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E]
    (f : ℝ → E → E) {tmin tmax : ℝ} (t₀ : Icc tmin tmax) (x₀ : E) (a r L K : ℝ≥0) : Prop where
  /-- The vector field at any time is Lipschitz with constant `K` within a closed ball. -/
  lipschitzOnWith : ∀ t ∈ Icc tmin tmax, LipschitzOnWith K (f t) (closedBall x₀ a)
  /-- The vector field is continuous in time within a closed ball. -/
  continuousOn : ∀ x ∈ closedBall x₀ a, ContinuousOn (f · x) (Icc tmin tmax)
  /-- `L` is an upper bound of the norm of the vector field. -/

nodes.name: ODE.FunSpace
nodes.lean:
structure FunSpace {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E]
    {tmin tmax : ℝ} (t₀ : Icc tmin tmax) (x₀ : E) (r L : ℝ≥0) where
  /-- The domain is `Icc tmin tmax`. -/
  toFun : Icc tmin tmax → E
  lipschitzWith : LipschitzWith L toFun
  mem_closedBall₀ : toFun t₀ ∈ closedBall x₀ r

nodes.name: ODE.FunSpace.instCompleteSpace
nodes.lean:
/-- We show that `FunSpace` is complete in order to apply the contraction mapping theorem. -/
instance [CompleteSpace E] : CompleteSpace (FunSpace t₀ x₀ r L) := by
  rw [completeSpace_iff_isComplete_range isUniformInducing_toContinuousMap]
  apply IsClosed.isComplete
  rw [range_toContinuousMap, ofPred_and]
  apply isClosed_setOfPred_lipschitzWith L |>.preimage continuous_coeFun |>.inter
  simp_rw [mem_closedBall_iff_norm]
  exact isClosed_le (by fun_prop) (by fun_prop)

nodes.name: ODE.picard
nodes.lean:
/-- The Picard iteration. It will be shown that if `α : ℝ → E` and `picard f t₀ x₀ α` agree on an
interval containing `t₀`, then `α` is a solution to `f` with `α t₀ = x₀` on this interval. -/
noncomputable def picard (f : ℝ → E → E) (t₀ : ℝ) (x₀ : E) (α : ℝ → E) : ℝ → E :=
  fun t ↦ x₀ + ∫ τ in t₀..t, f τ (α τ)

nodes.name: ODE.FunSpace.next
nodes.lean:
/-- The map on `FunSpace` defined by `picard`, some `n`-th iterate of which will be a contracting
map -/
noncomputable def next (hf : IsPicardLindelof f t₀ x₀ a r L K) (hx : x ∈ closedBall x₀ r)
    (α : FunSpace t₀ x₀ r L) : FunSpace t₀ x₀ r L where
  toFun t := picard f t₀ x α.compProj t
  lipschitzWith := LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul fun t₁ t₂ ↦ by
    rw [dist_eq_norm, picard_apply, picard_apply, add_sub_add_left_eq_sub,
      integral_interval_sub_left (intervalIntegrable_comp_compProj hf _ t₁)
        (intervalIntegrable_comp_compProj hf _ t₂), Subtype.dist_eq, Real.dist_eq]
    apply intervalIntegral.norm_integral_le_of_norm_le_const
    intro t ht
    -- Can `grind` do this in the future?
    have ht : t ∈ Icc tmin tmax :=
      subset_trans uIoc_subset_uIcc (uIcc_subset_Icc t₂.property t₁.property) ht
    exact hf.norm_le _ ht _ <| α.mem_closedBall hf.mul_max_le
  mem_closedBall₀ := by simp [hx]

/-- A time-dependent bound on the distance between the `n`-th iterates of `next` on two curves -/
lemma dist_iterate_next_apply_le (hf : IsPicardLindelof f t₀ x₀ a r L K)
    (hx : x ∈ closedBall x₀ r) (α β : FunSpace t₀ x₀ r L) (n : ℕ) (t : Icc tmin tmax) :
    dist ((next hf hx)^[n] α t) ((next hf hx)^[n] β t) ≤
      (K * |t.val - t₀.val|) ^ n / n ! * dist α β := by
  induction n generalizing t with
  | zero => simpa using!
      ContinuousMap.dist_apply_le_dist (f := toContinuousMap α) (g := toContinuousMap β) _
  | succ n hn =>
    rw [iterate_succ_apply', iterate_succ_apply', dist_eq_norm, next_apply,
      next_apply, picard_apply, picard_apply, add_sub_add_left_eq_sub,
      ← intervalIntegral.integral_sub (intervalIntegrable_comp_compProj hf _ t)
        (intervalIntegrable_comp_compProj hf _ t)]
    calc
      _ ≤ ∫ τ in uIoc t₀.val t.val, K ^ (n + 1) * |τ - t₀| ^ n / n ! * dist α β := by
        rw [intervalIntegral.norm_intervalIntegral_eq]
        apply MeasureTheory.norm_integral_le_of_norm_le (Continuous.integrableOn_uIoc (by fun_prop))
        apply ae_restrict_mem measurableSet_Ioc |>.mono
        intro t' ht'
        -- Can `grind` do this in the future?
        have ht' : t' ∈ Icc tmin tmax :=
          subset_trans uIoc_subset_uIcc (uIcc_subset_Icc t₀.property t.property) ht'
        rw [← dist_eq_norm, compProj_of_mem, compProj_of_mem]
        exact dist_comp_iterate_next_le hf hx _ ⟨t', ht'⟩ (hn _)
      _ ≤ (K * |t.val - t₀.val|) ^ (n + 1) / (n + 1) ! * dist α β := by
        apply le_of_abs_le
        -- critical: `integral_pow_abs_sub_uIoc`
        rw [← intervalIntegral.abs_intervalIntegral_eq, intervalIntegral.integral_mul_const,
          intervalIntegral.integral_div, intervalIntegral.integral_const_mul, abs_mul, abs_div,
          abs_mul, intervalIntegral.abs_intervalIntegral_eq, integral_pow_abs_sub_uIoc, abs_div,
          abs_pow, abs_pow, abs_dist, NNReal.abs_eq, abs_abs, mul_div, div_div, ← abs_mul,
          ← Nat.cast_succ, ← Nat.cast_mul, ← Nat.factorial_succ, Nat.abs_cast, ← mul_pow]

nodes.name: ODE.FunSpace.dist_iterate_next_iterate_next_le
nodes.lean:
/-- The `n`-th iterate of `next` is Lipschitz continuous with respect to `FunSpace`, with constant
$(K \max(t_{\mathrm{max}}, t_{\mathrm{min}})^n / n!$. -/
lemma dist_iterate_next_iterate_next_le (hf : IsPicardLindelof f t₀ x₀ a r L K)
    (hx : x ∈ closedBall x₀ r) (α β : FunSpace t₀ x₀ r L) (n : ℕ) :
    dist ((next hf hx)^[n] α) ((next hf hx)^[n] β) ≤
      (K * max (tmax - t₀) (t₀ - tmin)) ^ n / n ! * dist α β := by
  rw [← MetricSpace.isometry_induced FunSpace.toContinuousMap FunSpace.toContinuousMap.injective
    |>.dist_eq, ContinuousMap.dist_le]
  · intro t
    apply le_trans <| dist_iterate_next_apply_le hf hx α β n t
    gcongr
    exact abs_sub_le_max_sub t.property.1 t.property.2 _
  · have : 0 ≤ max (tmax - t₀) (t₀ - tmin) := le_max_of_le_left <| sub_nonneg_of_le t₀.property.2
    positivity

nodes.name: ODE.FunSpace.exists_contractingWith_iterate_next
nodes.lean:
/-- Some `n`-th iterate of `next` is a contracting map, and its associated Lipschitz constant is
independent of the initial point. -/
lemma exists_contractingWith_iterate_next (hf : IsPicardLindelof f t₀ x₀ a r L K) :
    ∃ (n : ℕ) (C : ℝ≥0), ∀ (x : E) (hx : x ∈ closedBall x₀ r),
      ContractingWith C (next hf hx)^[n] := by
  obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := FloorSemiring.tendsto_pow_div_factorial_atTop (K * max (tmax - t₀) (t₀ - tmin))
    |>.eventually (gt_mem_nhds zero_lt_one) |>.exists
  have : (0 : ℝ) ≤ (K * max (tmax - t₀) (t₀ - tmin)) ^ n / n ! := by
    have : 0 ≤ max (tmax - t₀) (t₀ - tmin) := le_max_of_le_left <| sub_nonneg_of_le t₀.property.2
    positivity
  refine ⟨n, ⟨_, this⟩, fun x hx ↦ ?_⟩
  exact ⟨hn, LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul fun α β ↦ dist_iterate_next_iterate_next_le hf hx α β n⟩

nodes.name: ContractingWith.isFixedPt_fixedPoint_iterate
nodes.lean:
theorem isFixedPt_fixedPoint_iterate {n : ℕ} (hf : ContractingWith K f^[n]) :
    IsFixedPt f (hf.fixedPoint f^[n]) := by
  set x := hf.fixedPoint f^[n]
  have hx : f^[n] x = x := hf.fixedPoint_isFixedPt
  have := hf.toLipschitzWith.dist_le_mul x (f x)
  rw [← iterate_succ_apply, iterate_succ_apply', hx] at this
  contrapose! this

nodes.name: ODE.FunSpace.exists_isFixedPt_next
nodes.lean:
/-- The map `next` has a fixed point in the space of curves. This will be used to construct a
solution `α : ℝ → E` to the ODE. -/
lemma exists_isFixedPt_next [CompleteSpace E] (hf : IsPicardLindelof f t₀ x₀ a r L K)
    (hx : x ∈ closedBall x₀ r) :
    ∃ α : FunSpace t₀ x₀ r L, IsFixedPt (next hf hx) α :=
  let ⟨_, _, h⟩ := exists_contractingWith_iterate_next hf
  ⟨_, h x hx |>.isFixedPt_fixedPoint_iterate⟩

nodes.name: ODE.FunSpace.compProj
nodes.lean:
/-- Extend the domain of `α` from `Icc tmin tmax` to `ℝ` such that `α t = α tmin` for all `t ≤ tmin`
and `α t = α tmax` for all `t ≥ tmax`. -/
noncomputable def compProj (α : FunSpace t₀ x₀ r L) (t : ℝ) : E :=
  α <| projIcc tmin tmax (le_trans t₀.property.1 t₀.property.2) t

/-- A time-reversed version of `ODE_solution_unique_of_mem_Icc_right`. Uniqueness is shown in a
closed interval `Icc a b`, where `b` is the "initial" time. -/
theorem ODE_solution_unique_of_mem_Icc_left
    (hv : ∀ t ∈ Ioc a b, LipschitzOnWith K (v t) (s t))
    (hf : ContinuousOn f (Icc a b))
    (hf' : ∀ t ∈ Ioc a b, HasDerivWithinAt f (v t (f t)) (Iic t) t)
    (hfs : ∀ t ∈ Ioc a b, f t ∈ s t)
    (hg : ContinuousOn g (Icc a b))
    (hg' : ∀ t ∈ Ioc a b, HasDerivWithinAt g (v t (g t)) (Iic t) t)
    (hgs : ∀ t ∈ Ioc a b, g t ∈ s t)
    (hb : f b = g b) :
    EqOn f g (Icc a b) := by
  have hv' : ∀ t ∈ Ico (-b) (-a), LipschitzOnWith K (Neg.neg ∘ (v (-t))) (s (-t)) := by
    intro t ht
    replace ht : -t ∈ Ioc a b := by
      push _ ∈ _ at ht ⊢
      constructor <;> linarith
    rw [← one_mul K]
    exact LipschitzWith.id.neg.comp_lipschitzOnWith (hv _ ht)
  have hmt1 : MapsTo Neg.neg (Icc (-b) (-a)) (Icc a b) :=
    fun _ ht ↦ ⟨le_neg.mp ht.2, neg_le.mp ht.1⟩
  have hmt2 : MapsTo Neg.neg (Ico (-b) (-a)) (Ioc a b) :=
    fun _ ht ↦ ⟨lt_neg.mp ht.2, neg_le.mp ht.1⟩
  have hmt3 (t : ℝ) : MapsTo Neg.neg (Ici t) (Iic (-t)) :=
    fun _ ht' ↦ mem_Iic.mpr <| neg_le_neg ht'
  suffices EqOn (f ∘ Neg.neg) (g ∘ Neg.neg) (Icc (-b) (-a)) by
    rw [eqOn_comp_right_iff] at this
    convert this
    simp
  apply ODE_solution_unique_of_mem_Icc_right hv'
    (hf.comp continuousOn_neg hmt1) _ (fun _ ht ↦ hfs _ (hmt2 ht))
    (hg.comp continuousOn_neg hmt1) _ (fun _ ht ↦ hgs _ (hmt2 ht)) (by simp [hb])
  · intro t ht
    convert
      HasFDerivWithinAt.comp_hasDerivWithinAt t (hf' (-t) (hmt2 ht))
        (hasDerivAt_neg t).hasDerivWithinAt (hmt3 t)
    simp
  · intro t ht
    convert
      HasFDerivWithinAt.comp_hasDerivWithinAt t (hg' (-t) (hmt2 ht))
        (hasDerivAt_neg t).hasDerivWithinAt (hmt3 t)
    simp

theorem dist_le_of_trajectories_ODE_of_mem
    (hv : ∀ t ∈ Ico a b, LipschitzOnWith K (v t) (s t))
    (hf : ContinuousOn f (Icc a b))
    (hf' : ∀ t ∈ Ico a b, HasDerivWithinAt f (v t (f t)) (Ici t) t)

nodes.name: norm_le_gronwallBound_of_norm_deriv_right_le
nodes.lean:
/-- A Grönwall-like inequality: if `f : ℝ → E` is continuous on `[a, b]`, has right derivative
`f' x` at every point `x ∈ [a, b)`, and satisfies the inequalities `‖f a‖ ≤ δ`,
`∀ x ∈ [a, b), ‖f' x‖ ≤ K * ‖f x‖ + ε`, then `‖f x‖` is bounded by `gronwallBound δ K ε (x - a)`
on `[a, b]`. -/
theorem norm_le_gronwallBound_of_norm_deriv_right_le {f f' : ℝ → E} {δ K ε : ℝ} {a b : ℝ}
    (hf : ContinuousOn f (Icc a b)) (hf' : ∀ x ∈ Ico a b, HasDerivWithinAt f (f' x) (Ici x) x)
    (ha : ‖f a‖ ≤ δ) (bound : ∀ x ∈ Ico a b, ‖f' x‖ ≤ K * ‖f x‖ + ε) :
    ∀ x ∈ Icc a b, ‖f x‖ ≤ gronwallBound δ K ε (x - a) :=
  le_gronwallBound_of_liminf_deriv_right_le (continuous_norm.comp_continuousOn hf)
    (fun x hx _r hr => (hf' x hx).liminf_right_slope_norm_le hr) ha bound

/-- Let `f : [a, b] → E` be a differentiable function such that `f a = 0`
and `‖f'(x)‖ ≤ K ‖f(x)‖` for some constant `K`. Then `f = 0` on `[a, b]`. -/
theorem eq_zero_of_abs_deriv_le_mul_abs_self_of_eq_zero_right {f f' : ℝ → E} {K a b : ℝ}
    (hf : ContinuousOn f (Icc a b)) (hf' : ∀ x ∈ Ico a b, HasDerivWithinAt f (f' x) (Ici x) x)
    (ha : f a = 0) (bound : ∀ x ∈ Ico a b, ‖f' x‖ ≤ K * ‖f x‖) :
    ∀ x ∈ Set.Icc a b, f x = 0 := by
  intro x hx
  apply norm_le_zero_iff.mp
  calc ‖f x‖
    _ ≤ gronwallBound 0 K 0 (x - a) :=
      norm_le_gronwallBound_of_norm_deriv_right_le hf hf' (by simp [ha]) (by simpa using bound) _ hx
    _ = 0 := by rw [gronwallBound_ε0_δ0]

variable {v : ℝ → E → E} {s : ℝ → Set E} {K : ℝ≥0} {f g f' g' : ℝ → E} {a b : ℝ} {εf εg δ : ℝ}

/-- If `f` and `g` are two approximate solutions of the same ODE, then the distance between them
can't grow faster than exponentially. This is a simple corollary of Grönwall's inequality, and some
people call this Grönwall's inequality too.

nodes.statement: E is a complete real normed space; the closed time interval I contains t₀.

On the closed ball around x₀ of radius a, the field is uniformly K-Lipschitz in state, continuous in time, and bounded by L. The interval size satisfies L·R ≤ a−r, where R is the greater distance from t₀ to an endpoint. The initial point x lies in the radius-r ball.
Use interval-valued Lipschitz curves with the initial-ball constraint and the supremum metric. Completeness follows by identifying a closed subset of continuous maps.
The admissible curve space X is a nonempty complete metric space.
Integrate the field along a candidate curve. The field bound and the interval-size hypothesis keep the construction admissible.
The Picard integral formula Tα(t)=x+∫ₜ₀ᵗ f(s,α(s)) ds defines a self-map T of the admissible curve space.
Induct on n, bound differences of vector-field values using Lipschitz continuity, integrate the power of elapsed time, then take the supremum over the interval.
The distance between Tⁿα and Tⁿβ is bounded by ((K·R)ⁿ/n!) times the distance between α and β.
Use convergence of (K·R)ⁿ/n! to zero to choose n with a Lipschitz coefficient less than one.
There is an iterate Tⁿ that is a contraction on the admissible curve space.

fact:state-space.title: Complete state space and initial time
fact:state-space.summary: The state space E is a complete real normed space and t₀ belongs to the closed time interval I.
fact:state-space.why_here: These are inputs to the curve-space construction and the verification of the derivative within I.

fact:existence-hypotheses.title: Field bounds and admissible initial state
fact:existence-hypotheses.summary: The field is K-Lipschitz in the state, continuous in time and bounded by L on the larger ball. The room between radii r and a accommodates the drift LR, and the chosen initial state x lies in the smaller ball.
fact:existence-hypotheses.why_here: These bounds keep Picard updates admissible, control differences between updates and allow differentiation of the integral along the fixed curve.

step:curve-space.title: Build a complete space of candidate curves
step:curve-space.summary: Use the supremum metric on E-valued curves over I with Lipschitz constant at most L and starting value in the radius-r ball. Uniform limits preserve the Lipschitz bound and the closed initial-ball constraint, so the space is closed in the complete continuous-map space. The constant curve at x₀ gives a member.
step:curve-space.why_here: It produces the admissible complete space on which the Picard update acts.

fact:curve-space.title: Nonempty complete space of admissible curves
fact:curve-space.summary: The admissible curve space X has a member and is complete in the supremum metric.
fact:curve-space.why_here: It gives the domain of the integral update and the complete space used by the fixed-point argument.

step:picard-self-map.title: Show that the Picard update preserves admissibility
step:picard-self-map.summary: An admissible input curve stays within distance r+LR of x₀, by its initial-ball condition and its L-Lipschitz bound. This is within the larger ball, so the field bound implies that integrating between any two output times yields a difference of norm at most L|t−s|. At t₀ the integral vanishes and the output equals x, so it is again an admissible curve.
step:picard-self-map.why_here: It makes repeated Picard updates possible on the same space.

fact:picard-self-map.title: Picard self-map on the curve space
fact:picard-self-map.summary: For the chosen x, the integral update defines a map T from the admissible curve space to itself.
fact:picard-self-map.why_here: It provides both the map to iterate and the formula to expand at a fixed point.

step:factorial-bound.title: Estimate repeated Picard updates
step:factorial-bound.summary: Start with the supremum distance between two admissible curves. After one more update, the common initial state cancels and the field Lipschitz bound gives K times the preceding pointwise difference under the integral. Integrating an elapsed-time power gives uⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) from uⁿ, producing the factorial by induction. Using the largest elapsed time R gives the estimate in the supremum metric.
step:factorial-bound.why_here: It supplies the bound from which a contracting iterate is chosen.

fact:factorial-bound.title: Lipschitz bound for the nth update
fact:factorial-bound.summary: The supremum distance between two curves after n updates is at most their original distance multiplied by (KR)ⁿ/n!.
fact:factorial-bound.why_here: The coefficient in this bound is the quantity made smaller than one.

step:contracting-iterate.title: Choose an iterate that shrinks distances
step:contracting-iterate.summary: The uniform distance bound has coefficient (KR)ⁿ/n!. Consecutive coefficients satisfy cₙ₊₁ = cₙ·KR/(n+1), so the coefficient tends to zero. Choose n with cₙ < 1 to obtain a contraction, with the same choice valid for every permitted x.
step:contracting-iterate.why_here: It turns the distance bound into the contraction needed for the fixed-point argument.

fact:contracting-iterate.title: A contracting Picard iterate
fact:contracting-iterate.summary: The Picard update under consideration has an iterate Tⁿ whose Lipschitz coefficient is strictly less than one.
fact:contracting-iterate.why_here: This is the contraction input to the fixed-curve construction.

step:fixed-curve.title: Find a curve fixed by the Picard update
step:fixed-curve.summary: Apply the contraction fixed-point theorem to Tⁿ on the complete admissible curve space. If α is its fixed point, then Tα is also fixed by Tⁿ because T and Tⁿ commute. Uniqueness of the fixed point of Tⁿ gives Tα = α.
step:fixed-curve.why_here: It produces the fixed curve from which the integral solution is built.

fact:fixed-curve.title: An admissible fixed curve
fact:fixed-curve.summary: For the chosen initial state, there exists an admissible curve α satisfying Tα = α.
fact:fixed-curve.why_here: The next step takes such a curve and expands its fixed-point identity.

step:integral-equation.title: Read the fixed-point identity as an integral equation
step:integral-equation.summary: Choose an admissible fixed curve α and extend it to a real-line function g by holding its endpoint values constant outside the interval. For t in the interval, g(t) equals α(t), which equals the value of Tα at t. The definition of Tα uses the extended curve g under the integral, giving the stated equation on I.
step:integral-equation.why_here: It gives an equation for the particular real-line witness used in the existence proof.

fact:integral-equation.title: Integral equation for the extended curve
fact:integral-equation.summary: The particular extended fixed curve g satisfies the Picard integral equation at every time in I.
fact:integral-equation.why_here: This equality gives the initial value and transfers the derivative of the integral expression to g.

step:ode-solution.title: Verify the initial value and the ODE
step:ode-solution.summary: Setting t = t₀ in the integral equation gives g(t₀) = x because the integral over a zero-length interval vanishes. The continuity and ball bounds allow the fundamental theorem of calculus to give the derivative of the integral expression within I as f(t,g(t)). Since g equals that expression on I, it has the same within-interval derivative there.
step:ode-solution.why_here: It verifies both requirements for the existential solution.

fact:ode-solution.title: Existence of a solution on the closed interval
fact:ode-solution.summary: Under the existence hypotheses, there is a real-line curve with the prescribed initial state and the required derivative within I at every time in I.
fact:ode-solution.compact_latex: \exists g:\mathbb R\to E,\quad g(t_0)=x\ \land\ \forall t\in I,\ \operatorname{HasDerivWithinAt}(g,f(t,g(t)),I,t)
fact:ode-solution.why_here: This is the explicit concluding assertion of the existence theorem.

fact:uniqueness-hypotheses.title: Interior equation and state constraints
fact:uniqueness-hypotheses.summary: The initial time t₀ lies strictly inside [a,b]. Both curves are continuous on the closed interval, satisfy the same ODE in its interior and lie in s(t) there, where the field has a common state Lipschitz bound.
fact:uniqueness-hypotheses.why_here: These hypotheses restrict to the half-intervals used in the two uniqueness applications.

fact:same-initial-value.title: Equal values at the initial time
fact:same-initial-value.summary: The two trajectories have zero separation at t₀.
fact:same-initial-value.why_here: This supplies the endpoint equality for both half-interval applications.

step:trajectory-comparison.title: Bound separation by Grönwall’s inequality
step:trajectory-comparison.summary: For two forward trajectories in the permitted sets, the right derivative of h = f−g is the difference of their field values, so ‖h′‖ ≤ K‖h‖ by the state Lipschitz bound. The exact-trajectory comparison uses the approximate-trajectory bound with zero errors. An initial distance at most δ then gives distance at most δ exp(K(t−a)) on the closed interval.
step:trajectory-comparison.why_here: It produces a reusable estimate that can be applied with zero initial separation.

fact:trajectory-comparison.title: Forward separation estimate
fact:trajectory-comparison.summary: Under the forward comparison hypotheses, initial distance at most δ gives an exponential bound on the distance at every time in [a,b].
fact:trajectory-comparison.why_here: It is the reusable premise specialized to equal initial values.

step:one-sided-principle.title: Deduce forward uniqueness from zero separation
step:one-sided-principle.summary: Equality at the left endpoint allows the forward separation estimate with δ = 0. Its upper bound is then zero at every time, and metric distance zero implies equality. This gives the reusable forward uniqueness principle under the one-sided hypotheses.
step:one-sided-principle.why_here: It converts a quantitative comparison into a one-sided uniqueness theorem.

fact:one-sided-principle.title: Reusable forward uniqueness principle
fact:one-sided-principle.summary: Under the one-sided equation, continuity, membership and Lipschitz hypotheses, equality at the left endpoint implies agreement on the entire forward interval.
fact:one-sided-principle.why_here: It supplies forward uniqueness directly and through time reversal.

step:split-interval.title: Restrict the hypotheses to the two halves
step:split-interval.summary: Since a < t₀ < b, the intervals [a,t₀] and [t₀,b] cover [a,b]. The derivative and field hypotheses are needed on (a,t₀] and [t₀,b), respectively, both of which lie inside (a,b). Restrict continuity to each closed half and use the ordinary derivatives to obtain the needed left or right derivatives.
step:split-interval.why_here: It prepares the hypotheses for the two one-sided applications and supplies the cover for the final conclusion.

fact:split-interval.title: Two covering halves with restricted hypotheses
fact:split-interval.summary: The two halves cover [a,b] and inherit the hypotheses for their respective one-sided uniqueness results.
fact:split-interval.why_here: It feeds both one-sided applications and identifies the union on which their conclusions combine.

step:forward-agreement.title: Apply forward uniqueness on the right half
step:forward-agreement.summary: On [t₀,b], the two curves have the required right derivatives and permitted state values at times in [t₀,b). Their equality at the left endpoint t₀ lets the forward theorem give agreement on all of [t₀,b].
step:forward-agreement.why_here: It produces the right-half equality used in the full-interval conclusion.

fact:forward-agreement.title: Agreement on the right half
fact:forward-agreement.summary: The two trajectories in the main theorem agree from t₀ through b.
fact:forward-agreement.why_here: This supplies equality at each point of the right half of the cover.

step:backward-agreement.title: Apply backward uniqueness on the left half
step:backward-agreement.summary: On [a,t₀], use the restricted left-derivative hypotheses and equality at the right endpoint t₀. The backward theorem follows by reflecting time: differentiating a reflected curve introduces a minus sign, so the reflected field is −v(−t,·), with the same state Lipschitz constant. Forward uniqueness on the reflected interval gives agreement back on [a,t₀].
step:backward-agreement.why_here: It produces the left-half equality used in the full-interval conclusion.

fact:backward-agreement.title: Agreement on the left half
fact:backward-agreement.summary: The two trajectories in the main theorem agree from a through t₀.
fact:backward-agreement.why_here: This supplies equality at each point of the left half of the cover.

step:agreement-on-interval.title: Combine equality on the two halves
step:agreement-on-interval.summary: Any t in [a,b] belongs to [a,t₀] or [t₀,b]. The corresponding half-interval equality gives f(t) = g(t), so the curves agree on the whole interval.
step:agreement-on-interval.why_here: It joins the particular forward and backward conclusions into the theorem’s assertion.

fact:agreement-on-interval.title: Agreement on the full interval
fact:agreement-on-interval.summary: Under the main uniqueness hypotheses, the two trajectories agree at every point of [a,b].
fact:agreement-on-interval.why_here: This is the explicit concluding assertion of the uniqueness theorem.

concepts.title: Complete space of admissible curves
concepts.summary: The supremum metric measures the largest pointwise distance between two curves. A common Lipschitz bound and a closed constraint at the initial time both survive uniform convergence, allowing completeness to pass from continuous maps to the constrained curves.

concepts.title: Picard integration
concepts.summary: Integrate the field along a candidate curve and add the initial state. A curve fixed by this update satisfies the integral equation for the ODE, from which differentiation recovers the differential equation.

concepts.title: Factorial decay under repeated integration
concepts.summary: Each integration of an elapsed-time power increases its exponent and divides by the new exponent. Iteration yields a factor 1/n!, which makes the Lipschitz bound tend to zero even for a fixed positive value of KR.

concepts.title: Contraction and fixed points
concepts.summary: A contraction on a nonempty complete metric space has a unique fixed point. When the contraction is an iterate Tⁿ, the map T sends that fixed point to another fixed point of Tⁿ, so uniqueness forces T to fix it as well.

concepts.title: Derivatives within a set
concepts.summary: A derivative within a set uses increments that stay in that set. For a closed interval this permits differentiation at the endpoints from the available side, and equality of two functions on the interval transfers any such derivative between them.

concepts.title: Grönwall comparison
concepts.summary: A differential growth bound gives an exponential bound on how far apart two solutions can move. With zero initial distance and zero derivative error, the growth bound forces their distance to remain zero.

concepts.title: Time reversal
concepts.summary: Replacing t by −t swaps the interval endpoints and exchanges right and left derivatives. The chain rule negates the reflected vector field, and negation preserves distances and hence the state Lipschitz constant.
